why: The greenhouse effect works on infrared radiation. About 60% of the Sun's radiation reaching the Earth is infrared (§13.3.3), and infrared is what the atmospheric greenhouse gases absorb and re-radiate, so the Earth's atmosphere is heated by it. Visible light passes through the atmosphere largely unabsorbed and is not what the greenhouse gases trap; X-rays from the Sun are absorbed high in the atmosphere and carry a negligible share of the solar power; microwaves form only a tiny part of the solar output and are not a greenhouse carrier. The correct choice is therefore infra-red radiation.

Of the radiation present in the Earth's atmosphere, infrared is by far the most abundant: the chapter states that about 60% of the solar radiation is infrared in nature (§13.3.3), and every warm body in the atmosphere — air, cloud, ground — is itself an infrared emitter, since all hot bodies are sources of infrared rays. Ultraviolet is largely stripped out by the ozone layer, X-rays from space are absorbed high up and never reach the lower atmosphere in quantity, and microwaves are only a very small fraction of the solar spectrum. The atmosphere is therefore richest in infrared radiation.

The frequency of a wave is set by its source and does not change when the wave enters a new medium; what changes is the speed and hence the wavelength. In a medium of refractive index \( n \) the speed becomes \( v = c/n \), and since \( v = \nu\lambda \) must still hold with \( \nu \) fixed, the wavelength shortens to \( \lambda/n \). So an ultraviolet beam entering glass keeps the same frequency it had in air. Note on the printed question: two of the four printed alternatives — 'No change' and 'remains same' — say exactly the same thing, so the correct statement appears twice and the physics cannot single out one letter. The first-listed of the two equivalent alternatives is recorded here; a student who picked the other is equally right.

Characteristic (2) of an EM wave is that the cross product of the electric and magnetic field vectors, \( \vec{E} \times \vec{B} \), points along the direction in which the wave travels and also gives the energy carried by the wave. The scalar product \( \vec{E} \cdot \vec{B} \) is a number, not a vector, and cannot specify a direction at all — and in an EM wave it is zero anyway, because the two fields are mutually perpendicular. The wave is transverse, so it travels perpendicular to both fields and cannot propagate along either one of them. The direction of travel is therefore given by the cross product of the electric and magnetic fields.

For a transmitting antenna of height \( h \) on an Earth of radius \( R \), the line-of-sight range is \( d = \sqrt{2Rh} \) — obtained from the right triangle in Fig. 13.5, where \( (R + h)^{2} = d^{2} + R^{2} \) and \( h^{2} \) is dropped because \( h \ll R \). Since \( 2R \) is a constant, \( d \propto \sqrt{h} \), i.e. the range varies as \( h^{1/2} \). Doubling the tower height therefore multiplies the range by \( \sqrt{2} \), not by 2, so a linear, three-halves or square dependence is ruled out. The correct proportionality is to the square root of the height.

Communication satellites are reached by microwaves. Radio waves of frequency above about 30 MHz pass straight through the ionosphere (§13.4.2), so a wave sent up to a satellite and back must lie well above that limit, and the microwave band satisfies it; §13.3.2 lists long-distance telephone communication and the transmission of TV signals among the uses of microwaves. The AM broadcast band (530-1710 kHz) is reflected or absorbed long before it reaches a satellite and is used for ground-wave broadcasting, while the FM broadcast band is allocated to terrestrial radio rather than to satellite links. X-rays are absorbed by the atmosphere and are ionising, so they are unusable for communication. The waves used are microwaves.

The line-of-sight coverage radius of a transmitting antenna of height \( h \) is \( d = \sqrt{2Rh} \), so the height needed for a required radius is \( h = \dfrac{d^{2}}{2R} \). Here \( d = 640\ \text{km} = 6.4 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m} \), and the chapter uses \( R = 6.4 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m} \) for the Earth throughout (Solved Ex.13.7 and 13.9). Hence \( h = \dfrac{(6.4 \times 10^{5})^{2}}{2 \times 6.4 \times 10^{6}} = \dfrac{4.096 \times 10^{11}}{1.28 \times 10^{7}} = 3.2 \times 10^{4}\ \text{m} \), that is 32000 m. The stem does not itself state the radius of the Earth; the value above is the one the chapter uses.
